title: Chapter 1 — Cool Hearts
paragraphs: Julia moves in with Mae Daeng and Goy. The household's rhythm — pre-dawn trips to the market stall, shared meals, gentle collisions over showers and shared rooms — becomes her first classroom. Goy, quiet and decisive, runs most things; Mae Daeng talks nonstop in the Northern dialect and takes her new lodger everywhere.

The chapter's subject is the town's emotional weather. Julia arrived trained on ethnographies of dramatic feeling — rage, grief, headhunters' fury — and instead finds calm, everywhere, all the time. The valley's word for it is jai yen: the cool heart.

Afternoons pass at Gaew's shop, trading English lessons for Thai ones while Sen minds the counter and Aung — pork vendor, disco-goer, the liveliest person in any room — comes and goes. When the festival committee votes to commercialize the town's weaving, Goy objects once and then simply leaves, cool to the last. When a customer sees Julia rushing, the advice is two words: jai yen.

Cool-heartedness is practiced at the wat as much as preached: cousin Jip's nighttime ordination parade is boisterous and yet unmistakably calm; the weekly wan phra brings the neighborhood to Wat Ko with offerings; and interviewees from the police chief on down describe themselves, aspirationally, as jai yen.

To ask the valley systematically, Goy recommends Ari — a local Karen man with a master's thesis, a boardinghouse full of village schoolchildren, and a battered Toyota. Together he and Julia build an eighteen-question interview and begin with P'Dao, Goy's aunt at the administration office, then widen to the jungle hamlet of Chang Kao, thirty kilometers down a dirt road.

The interviews return one lesson again and again: asked about loss — a failed crop, a stolen note, a death — people do not narrate feelings; they narrate letting the feeling go. The cool heart, the chapter argues, is not suppression of some universal inner heat. It is a cultivated, moral orientation — and the doctrine of impermanence is its quiet engine.
